bp: Many web systems now place a general-purpose AI model between people and information. A search engine may use it to understand a query, a recommender may use it to choose what appears next, and a social-media analytics tool may use it to summarize public behavior. The useful promise is that one broad model can serve many tasks. The danger is that one broad model can also carry hidden unfairness, unclear reasoning, fragile behavior, or mistaken cause-and-effect stories into many tasks at once. This paper is a workshop proposal about that pressure. It argues that trustworthiness for web intelligence cannot be checked only by asking whether the model usually gives a good answer. The web data behind these models is massive, mixed in type, and constantly changing. The workshop's central claim is that causal reasoning, meaning careful thinking about what actually changes what, can give researchers a more disciplined way to evaluate and improve these models.
wh: The hard part is that web-scale models learn from the same kind of environment in which they will later be judged: noisy, mixed, social, commercial, fast-changing, and full of unequal visibility. A model may notice that certain users click certain items, that some groups appear with some words, or that one kind of content spreads quickly. Those patterns can help prediction, but they may not explain why the outcome happened. Maybe users clicked because the item was shown more often. Maybe a group is associated with a label because the training data overrepresented one source. Maybe a ranking looks successful because it learned past exposure rather than present preference. Trustworthiness also has several meanings at once: fairness, transparency, causality, and ability to keep working under new conditions. A simple score cannot easily say which of these failed, whether the failure is local or systemic, or how a repair would change the deployed web system.
naive: A smart beginner might test a foundation model by running it on many web tasks and keeping the version with the best average accuracy, click prediction, or ranking score. They might add separate checklists for fairness, explainability, and reliability after training. This fails because a model can score well while relying on the wrong reason. It can recommend popular items because they were historically overexposed, not because they are best for a user. It can produce a fluent explanation that hides a biased shortcut. It can pass one static test and fail when web data, user behavior, or platform incentives change. The naive approach treats trust as an output label. The workshop frames it as a question about the process that produced the output.
ap: The paper's core move is to put causal reasoning at the center of trustworthy foundation models for web intelligence. Instead of asking only, "Did the model predict correctly?", causal reasoning asks, "What would change if this input, exposure, source, user attribute, ranking rule, or training signal changed while the important alternatives stayed comparable?" That shift matters because web systems are action systems. Search results are shown, recommendations allocate attention, and social-media analytics can influence decisions about people or content. A trustworthy model therefore needs more than surface success. It needs ways to identify which observed patterns are useful evidence and which are accidents of data collection, platform feedback, or social bias. As a workshop, the contribution is not one finished method. It is a focused forum for bringing fairness, transparency, causality, and reliability work together around this cause-and-effect lens.
mech: The mechanism described by the abstract is a research workflow rather than a single algorithm. The input is a set of critical web applications that already rely on foundation models: search, recommendation, and social-media analytics are named examples. The next input is the data environment behind them: heterogeneous web records, changing behavior, and very large scale. The first step is to identify where trust can fail. Fairness asks whether errors or benefits are unevenly distributed. Transparency asks whether people can inspect why a model behaved as it did. Causality asks whether the model has learned drivers of outcomes or only things that travel with those drivers. Reliability under change asks whether behavior stays acceptable when the web setting shifts. The second step is to turn those concerns into causal questions. For a recommender, one question might be whether exposure caused an item to look desirable. For search, it might be whether a ranking change caused better satisfaction or merely followed easier queries. For social analytics, it might be whether a measured group pattern reflects real behavior or biased observation. The third step is evaluation and enhancement: compare situations carefully, look for misleading companions, design tests that separate cause from coincidence, and use those findings to guide model repair. The output is a research agenda and shared set of challenges for trustworthy web intelligence.
math: The main mathematical idea is causal comparison. Ordinary prediction asks whether past examples let us guess a future label, click, ranking, or summary. Causal reasoning asks a stricter question: if one part of the system were changed, would the outcome change because of that part? This requires imagining two comparable situations, one with the suspected driver and one without it. Since the same user, query, or platform moment cannot usually be observed in both versions, the comparison must be constructed from data, assumptions, interventions, or carefully chosen controls. Probability enters because the missing comparison is uncertain; repeated cases give evidence, but never perfect certainty. Ranking and recommendation add another mathematical object: an ordered list that changes what people see, which then changes the future data the model learns from. Fairness adds group comparison: benefits and errors must be measured across people who may not have had equal exposure in the first place. Transparency adds explanation as a compression problem: the system must reduce a huge model decision into a human-checkable account without losing the key reason. The tradeoff is actionability versus assumption. Causal math gives more useful guidance than correlation only when the constructed comparison really blocks the misleading alternative explanations.
dots: This paper sits where several recurring conference threads meet. It connects to causal-inference work because it treats prediction as inadequate when a platform will act on the answer. It connects to recommendation and ranking because search and recommender systems do not merely reflect user behavior; they shape what users see, which then shapes later data. It connects to misinformation and trust work because fluent model outputs and polished explanations can look reliable even when the evidence chain is weak. It also touches graph and social-media analysis, where links among users, posts, sources, and communities can carry useful evidence but can also spread bias or interference. The repo's causal-family data frames this shared problem as repairing broken comparisons: separating true drivers from passengers that only appear with them. The workshop brings that same view to foundation models, whose broad reuse makes each broken comparison more consequential.
ww: The causal perspective helps because many trust failures are errors of explanation, not only errors of prediction. A model trained on web data can learn that two things appear together and use that pairing successfully for a while. But if the pairing came from unequal exposure, platform design, missing sources, or old behavior, the model may fail or act unfairly when the setting changes. Causal reasoning pushes researchers to ask what produced the data before trusting the pattern. That matters for fairness because a group difference may reflect bias in observation rather than a real difference in need or behavior. It matters for transparency because an explanation should name the factor that made the decision move, not merely a feature that was correlated with it. It matters for reliability because causes are more likely than surface correlations to survive a new time period, new user group, or new platform rule. The abstract does not claim this solves trustworthiness by itself. Its stronger point is that cause-and-effect thinking gives the scattered trust problems a common language.
po: The payoff is a clearer research agenda for models that increasingly sit inside critical web infrastructure. If the workshop succeeds, researchers working on fairness, transparency, reliability, and web-scale modeling can compare their problems through a shared causal lens instead of treating them as separate checklists. For builders of search, recommendation, and social-media analytics systems, the practical benefit is better questions: what pattern is the model using, what action will follow, who may be harmed, and what evidence shows the action changes the intended outcome? Grounded in the abstract, the result is a forum and challenge map, not a reported new deployed system.
limits: Because this is a workshop abstract, it does not provide experiments, datasets, algorithms, or measured improvements. It names causal reasoning as a principled direction, but it does not prove which causal tools work best for foundation models on web data. Any causal evaluation will depend on hard assumptions: that important variables were observed, that comparison groups are fair enough, that interventions are meaningful, and that the web system does not change in response to the test. The abstract also groups fairness, transparency, causality, and reliability together, but it does not show how to resolve conflicts among them in deployment.
